hypothesis: H0: Trip duration is normally distributed
conclusion: Duration is strongly right-skewed (skewness = 0.96) and rejects normality (W = 0.9172, p < 2.2e-16). Non-parametric testing is strictly warranted.

hypothesis: H0: Trip duration distributions are equal across members and casual riders
conclusion: Casual riders ride significantly longer than annual members (median 11.82 min vs. 8.53 min; W = 8.83e+09, p < 2.2e-16; rank-biserial r = -0.250; Bootstrap 95% CI for median difference: [3.00, 3.68] mins).

hypothesis: H0: Trip duration distributions are identical across all 7 days of the week
conclusion: Trip duration varies significantly across days of the week (H = 590.47, df = 6, p < 2.2e-16), but the overall effect size is modest (epsilon^2 = 0.0020), driven by longer weekend leisure rides.

hypothesis: H0: Membership type and rideable bike type are independent
conclusion: Rider membership and bike type are significantly associated (Chi-sq = 1436.82, df = 1, p < 2.2e-16; Cramer's V = 0.0692). Annual members show distinct hardware adoption compared to casual visitors.

hypothesis: H0: Hourly trip volume distributions are identical on weekdays and weekends
conclusion: Hourly trip demand does not significantly differ in overall median volume between weekdays and weekends (median 6,876 vs. 4,507 trips/h; W = 61906.00, p = 0.0035; rank-biserial r = -0.137), though temporal shapes differ markedly.
